PHSCS 587

Quasi-Fermi levels

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how an electron–hole population above equilibrium appears as a level splitting

An operating junction can have electrons and holes that each relax internally while remaining out of mutual equilibrium. Their populations can then be described by electron and hole quasi-Fermi levels EFn and EFp. In a nondegenerate local model, n = NC exp[−(EC − EFn)/(kBT)] and p = NV exp[−(EFp − EV)/(kBT)]. All energies use the same reference.

Multiplication gives np = ni² exp[(EFn − EFp)/(kBT)]. At equilibrium EFn = EFp = EF and the ordinary mass-action product returns. A positive splitting EFn − EFp corresponds to a carrier product above equilibrium. The splitting is an energy; dividing by q expresses its voltage equivalent.

Spatial quasi-Fermi-level gradients describe the electrochemical driving forces for current under the transport assumptions. In an ideal forward-biased junction, the edge populations can be related to an applied voltage through an approximately qV splitting. Contact resistance, recombination and high injection can change this relationship, so the terminal voltage and every local splitting need not coincide.

Example

A splitting of kBT gives np = e·ni² in the nondegenerate local model. This specifies the product; neutrality, injection conditions and boundary conditions are needed to find n and p individually.

Practice

1. What does a single flat Fermi level imply about the equilibrium carrier product?

Set EFn − EFp to zero.

The exponential becomes one, giving np = ni² within the nondegenerate equilibrium model.
